source.title: The Birth of Knowledge: Emergent Features across Time, Space, and Scale in Large Language Models
source.authors: Shashata Sawmya; Micah Adler; N. Shavit

page_placements.theme: Representations and information observables scale differently from mean loss

record.file_problem: The text contains apparent cutoffs: a sentence in Section 5 ends mid-thought, and the History bullet in Section 6.2 is unfinished. The rest of the paper and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures interpretable-feature activation, not held-out cross-entropy loss or compute-optimal allocation. It cites scaling-law work but does not test or rely on those laws.
record.gate_note: The scale sweep reports categorical-feature activation, a different construct from every claim version. Those scale findings are recorded as none rather than as tests of a loss-scaling version. Kaplan et al. is cited in Related Work; no cited results are treated as this study's own results.
record.test_reason: The study measures SAE categorical-feature activation on MMLU prompts across Pythia checkpoints, layers and sizes. It reports no pretraining loss, no compute-optimal allocation and no downstream task performance. Kaplan et al. is cited only in Related Work. Its scale results concern a different construct from every version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors say interpretable categorical features emerge at specific thresholds in training time and model scale, and that layer-wise organisation is non-monotonic, with early-layer features re-emerging at the final layers. They call the work primarily descriptive.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE-based feature activation analysis; it does not measure the original scaling-law loss recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper notes that its SAE choice and concept-matching criteria constrain which feature dynamics are captured.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE-probed categorical-concept activation in Pythia jumps from under 5% to about 95% between 160M and 410M parameters, then plateaus. Business rises more gradually, stabilising above 1B. Over training, activation in Pythia-12B rises non-monotonically, with a 31.8 pp dip between 20k and 30k steps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Internal interpretable-feature coverage shows threshold-like rather than smooth power-law growth with scale and training steps.

record.problems: The authors describe the analysis as primarily descriptive and note that the SAE and concept-matching criteria may miss other feature dynamics. The scale results concern feature activation rather than loss, and no uncertainty estimates are stated for those results.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported scale-activation result left out. Other temporal and spatial feature analyses were not recorded because they do not bear on the parameter-scaling loss versions.

untested.parts: Held-out loss vs parameters, tokens or compute; power-law form.
Extrapolation of fitted laws to larger runs.
Effect of architecture shape on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power laws in other modalities or regimes.
Downstream task performance vs scale or loss. MMLU is used only as prompt text; no accuracy is measured.
Dependence of exponents or allocation on setup and fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The threshold-like activation curve is not evidence against the power-law loss versions, because it measures a different construct with an SAE trained only on the 12B model. Smaller models are mapped into the 12B space by Procrustes rotation, so the results depend on that alignment. The temporal results are not recorded as rows; this is acceptable because they too concern feature activation, not loss.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law form and range.
Whether loss laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its scaling with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream-task performance predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices.

relation.reason: Kaplan et al. is cited as background; the study neither tests nor operationally uses its scaling laws.

tranche.reason: The results measure categorical SAE feature activation, not pretraining loss, power-law extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream task performance. No claim version is tested or used as a tool.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. Cross-scale activations are aligned to the 12B reference using Procrustes rotation; activation saturation does not test a loss scaling law.
